questions.topic: The gold ground of the San Vitale apse, Ravenna

questions.stem: A graph of the San Vitale apse plots the number of gold-leaf tesserae per square centimetre across the apse, and the line falls steadily from the conch to the dado. What does the falling line indicate about the gold ground?

options.text: The gold tesserae were set more densely where the field was most visible and costly to cover
The gold was laid on in horizontal bands, with each band thinner than the one above
options.misconception: reads a density trend as a change of working method

options.text: The upper part of the apse was re-gilded in a later campaign that used less gold
options.misconception: turns a density gradient into a dated campaign

options.text: The apse was left unfinished above the conch, and the rest of the curve is later repair
options.misconception: reads lower density as evidence of an unfinished surface

questions.explanation: A falling line on a density graph shows the gold was set more closely where the surface mattered most. Bands, later campaigns and unfinished areas would each produce a different pattern from a smooth gradient.
questions.hint: Ask where the artist spent the most gold, and why there.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The youthful shepherd in the Galla Placidia mosaics, Ravenna
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a graph of relative figure sizes can and cannot show
questions.stem: A graph of the figures in the Galla Placidia mosaics shows the shepherd's head larger than every other head in the scene. Explain what a graph of relative figure sizes can and cannot tell you about a mosaic.

answer.exemplar: A graph of relative sizes shows the hierarchy the artist chose: the shepherd dominates the flock because he matters to the story, or because a hierarchy of scale was in use. What the graph cannot show is why that choice was made, whether the shepherd was meant as a portrait, or how the figures stand in space, since all of that lies in pictorial convention rather than in the measurement itself.

questions.explanation: A graph of relative sizes shows the hierarchy the artist chose, and here the shepherd dominates the flock. It cannot show the reason for the choice, nor how the figures occupy space, since that lies in convention.
questions.hint: Ask what a measured size leaves out of the picture.

questions.topic: Continuous narrative in the Vienna Genesis
questions.learningObjective: Identify a continuous narrative from a graph of scene counts and repeated figures

stimulus.body: A curator's graph for the Vienna Genesis plots the number of distinct scenes on each of six successive pages, rising from two on the first page to nine on the sixth. The caption notes that the figure of the same character appears more than once on several pages, and that the background is continuous across the page breaks. The catalogue entry must describe the narrative method from this graph.

questions.stem: A curator's graph of the Vienna Genesis plots scene counts rising from two to nine across six pages. Which catalogue description best fits the graph?

options.text: An illustrated list, in which each page carries one episode and the figures are never repeated
options.misconception: treats repeated figures as if they were never repeated

options.text: A set of separate framed scenes, each with its own figures and its own background
options.misconception: reads rising scene counts as a series of independent panels

options.text: A continuous narrative, in which several episodes of one story share a single field and repeat figures
A progressive copy, in which each page shows the same episode at an earlier and later stage
options.misconception: confuses repetition of characters with repetition of a single episode

questions.explanation: Scene counts rise while the same characters recur and the ground runs unbroken, which is what a continuous narrative does. Framed panels, one episode per page, and a repeated episode would each look different.
questions.hint: Ask what the rising count does to the space on the page.

options.text: That ornament and text are inversely related, so the most ornate pages carry the least writing
options.misconception: invents a fixed ratio between ornament and writing

options.text: That ornament is spread evenly, and every page was planned to the same density from the start
options.misconception: reads a flat line as evidence of uniform planning

options.text: That the most decorated folios are the latest, since decoration was added as the book was used
options.misconception: reads decoration added later as if the design were planned later

options.text: That ornament concentrates in the opening folios, and that the pages they govern are most treated

questions.explanation: Both lines peak together in the opening quires, where a frontispice and its initials belong, so ornament marks the start of a text rather than the age of a page. Even spread and accumulation are other patterns.
questions.hint: Look at where the two lines peak together.

questions.topic: The gold ground of the San Vitale apse, Ravenna
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a rising gold-to-colour ratio matters for reading the apse
questions.stem: A plot of the gold-to-colour ratio in the San Vitale apse shows the ratio rising sharply in the conch. Explain why a rising ratio in that graph matters for reading the mosaic.

answer.exemplar: A rising ratio of gold to coloured tesserae means the upper curve of the apse is almost entirely a field of light, with figure and drapery picked out in coloured glass. That is the visual claim of the conch: the space of the sanctuary is flooded with reflected light so that the enthroned figure is set against an unearthly, immaterial field rather than against a landscape or a room.

questions.explanation: A rising gold ratio means the upper curve is almost entirely a field of reflected light, with figures picked out in colour, so the sacred scene stands against something immaterial.
questions.hint: Ask what fills the upper curve of the apse.

questions.topic: The youthful shepherd in the Galla Placidia mosaics, Ravenna
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a recurring measured figure is a type or a portrait

stimulus.body: A conservator's graph of the Galla Placidia mosaics plots the height of each figure in a shepherd scene, and the shepherd's figure stands at 22 cm where the sheep range from 6 to 9 cm. A second series records the shepherd in three other scenes at 19, 21 and 20 cm. The report asks whether the shepherd is a portrait likeness or a type.

questions.stem: A conservator's graph of the Galla Placidia mosaics shows the shepherd tall in one scene and of similar height in three others. Which conclusion does the graph support?

options.text: The shepherd is simply a larger animal, since the graph gives no scale for the figures
options.misconception: ignores the scale the graph supplies for the figures

options.text: The figure is a portrait, since a specific person's height would be recorded consistently across scenes
options.misconception: reads a recurring height as evidence of a portrait likeness

options.text: The figure is a recurring type rather than a portrait, since the height recurs while the scenes differ
The graph settles the identity of the figure, since a measured height identifies a person
options.misconception: believes a measured height can identify a person

questions.explanation: The height recurs across different scenes, suggesting a conventional type rather than a particular sitter, and a measured height cannot establish identity. The figure is plainly a person, not an animal.
questions.hint: Ask whether the same height belongs to one person or to a role.

options.text: Establish that the halo is the earliest area painted, then assume the cheek was finished last of all
options.misconception: assumes a sequence of painting from a difference in thickness

options.text: Establish that the gold is thinner, then conclude the whole panel was repainted at a later date
options.misconception: infers a later campaign from a difference in thickness

options.text: Establish that the icon is larger than the other panels, then treat the thicker paint as better quality
options.misconception: reads panel size as an explanation of paint handling

options.text: Establish that the paint is built up in strokes, then show the strokes follow flesh and not the ground

questions.explanation: Painterly handling means the paint is laid in visible strokes and those strokes describe flesh. Thickness alone shows that one area carries more paint, and reveals no sequence or campaign.
questions.hint: Ask what the strokes are doing, not how deep the paint is.

questions.stem: A graph of the Vienna Genesis plots the number of figures per page beside the number of scene boundaries on that page. Which reading of the graph best explains the result?

options.text: Figures and boundaries rise together, because every episode in the manuscript is marked by a frame
options.misconception: assumes every episode in the manuscript is separately framed

options.text: Figures rise faster than boundaries, because one field can hold several episodes before it is divided
Boundaries rise faster than figures, because the artist drew more dividers than subjects
options.misconception: reads a rising count of dividers as extra subjects

options.text: The two lines never meet, because narrative and division are independent of one another
options.misconception: assumes narrative and division never interact

questions.explanation: When figures outpace boundaries, several episodes share one undivided field, which is the defining move of a continuous narrative. Equal rates would mean separate frames.

Forty-six per cent, because 46 is the largest of the six figures on the graph

options.misconception: reports the total and never divides by the count

questions.stem: Counting the figures on the Sanchi stupa gateway, a graph shows the highest number in the lowest register. Explain what that distribution suggests about how the gateway was planned.

answer.exemplar: A crowded lowest register suggests the plan began with a dense band of narrative close to the ground, where a visitor standing before the torana would meet the story at eye level, and that the upper bands were added as fillers and as an upward crescendo. The graph cannot by itself tell us the order of the campaigns, since a count of figures records density and not the date of the carving.

questions.explanation: A crowded lowest band suggests the plan began with dense narrative at the level of a standing visitor and built upward from there. A count of figures records density, not the order of the campaigns.

options.misconception: reads a change in density as a change in the artist's plan

options.text: The gold was removed from the lower part of the apse in a later campaign of stripping
options.misconception: reads a density gradient as the record of a stripping campaign

options.text: The gold and the coloured glass divide a roughly fixed area, with more of one leaving less of the other
The dado was decorated in a heavier medium that reflects more light per tessera
options.misconception: invents a change of medium to explain a graph of counts

questions.explanation: The two lines mirror each other, so a fixed area is shared between gold and coloured glass. No stripping campaign, unfinished zone or change of medium explains a smooth mirror in the data.

answer.exemplar: A rising scene count with a constant number of characters is the signature of a single story unfolded across the page. answer.exemplar: A ratio that holds steady across several scenes means the difference is a rule of the composition rather than a fact about one animal and one shepherd. questions.explanation: A ratio constant across several scenes is a compositional rule rather than a fact about one shepherd and one flock. The graph confirms a consistent convention, not a chance arrangement.

answer.exemplar: A denser gold field behind the enthroned figure tells the viewer that the surface behind Christ is not the same substance as the surface behind the attendants, and the artist has spent more material and more light on the place where the sacred presence sits. The graph itself records only the density; the meaning comes from what the convention of hierarchy made of such a difference, and it does not record why the choice was made or who paid for it.

questions.explanation: A denser gold field behind the enthroned figure marks him as the focus of the hierarchy, since more light and material sit behind him. The graph records density; the convention carries the meaning.

answer.exemplar: Bands that grow taller as they climb make the gateway open out as it rises, so the upper story carries more figures and more incident than the crowded base. The graph records the heights; the effect on the viewer is a matter of how the eye travels.

questions.topic: The youthful shepherd in the Galla Placidia mosaics, Ravenna
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a constant flock count alongside changing animals implies
questions.stem: Counting animals in the Galla Placidia mosaics, a graph shows that the number of sheep stays constant across three scenes while the number of other animals changes. Explain what that pattern implies about the flock.

answer.exemplar: A flock that stays at the same size while the surrounding variety of animals changes tells the reader that the sheep are a fixed element of the composition, present in each scene as a sign of the flock, while the other animals serve whatever the episode requires. The reader is therefore meant to read the sheep as a constant and the changing animals as variable, which is a narrative instruction rather than a record of a real pasture.

questions.explanation: A constant flock with changing other animals makes the sheep a fixed element of the composition and the rest variable, which tells the reader how to read the scene. The graph records the counts, not the reasons.
questions.hint: Ask which of the counted groups stays fixed across the scenes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Continuous narrative in the Vienna Genesis
questions.learningObjective: Read a narrowing ground band as a division of shared space

stimulus.body: A curator's graph for the Vienna Genesis plots the width of the continuous ground band against the number of episodes sharing it. Where five episodes share a band the band is narrow, and where two episodes share it the band is broad. The catalogue entry must describe the relation the graph reveals.

questions.stem: Charting the ground of the Vienna Genesis, a curator's table sets the width of the continuous band against the number of episodes sharing it, with a narrow band for five episodes and a broad one for two. Which relation does the graph reveal?

options.text: That the band narrows where the figures grow, because the figures need room
options.misconception: attributes a change in the ground to the size of the figures

options.text: That the ground is narrowest where the artists were most practised at dividing it
options.misconception: explains a measurement by the skill of the artists

options.text: That the number of episodes was fixed by the width of the ground available
options.misconception: reverses the relation between the ground and the episodes

options.text: That the ground is divided in proportion to the number of episodes it has to carry

questions.explanation: A band that narrows as the episodes multiply shows the ground shared out in proportion to what it carries. Skill, a fixed supply of ground and figure size are readings the graph does not carry.
questions.hint: Ask what the band is doing as the number of episodes rises.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Silver ink and decorative initials in the Rossano Gospels
questions.learningObjective: Set out the conditions for reading two inks as a hierarchy
questions.stem: Setting the two inks side by side, a graph of the Rossano Gospels shows silver-ink letters beside gold-leaf letters on each folio. Which two steps does a reader need before the two inks are read as a hierarchy?

options.text: Show that the gold is older than the silver, then treat the older ink as the more important one
options.misconception: equates the age of an ink with its importance in the design

options.text: Show that the gold is used sparingly, then show that it marks positions of importance in the text
Show that the two inks were bought separately, then treat the cost of each as the design rule
options.misconception: explains a visual hierarchy by the cost of the materials

options.text: Show that the gold was added at a later date, then treat the later ink as the decorative one
options.misconception: reads a later addition as a decorative intention

questions.explanation: Two inks form a hierarchy only if the sparing use of the gold is shown and its marking of important positions is shown. The age, cost and date of the inks describe something else.
questions.hint: Ask how much gold there is and what it is put on.

questions.topic: The registers of a Sanchi stupa gateway
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a wider spread of subjects in one band of a gateway
questions.stem: Comparing the three architraves of the Sanchi stupa gateway, a graph shows the middle band carrying the widest range of subject matter. Which reading of that spread is best supported?

options.text: That the middle band was added last, when the masons had the widest choice of models
options.misconception: infers a later addition from the variety of subjects

options.text: That the middle band was reserved for the least important episodes in the cycle
options.misconception: reads a wide range of subjects as low importance

options.text: That the gateway's subjects are distributed across the bands rather than confined to one of them
That the outer bands were left blank by mistake and filled in later
options.misconception: explains the spread by an error in the carving

questions.explanation: A wider range of subjects in the middle band shows the gateway's subjects are spread across the bands rather than kept in one. The graph shows no chronology, ranking or accident.
questions.hint: Ask where the variety of subjects is concentrated.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The four hands of the Chola bronze of Shiva as Lord of Dance
questions.learningObjective: Find the difference between the longest and shortest recorded arms
questions.stem: Of the Chola bronze of Shiva as Lord of Dance, a graph plots the four arms at 72, 60, 60 and 48 cm. What is the difference between the longest arm and the shortest?

options.text: Six centimetres, because the two arms of 60 cm are set 6 cm apart in the second reading
options.misconception: compares two arms that the graph gives as equal

options.text: One hundred and eighty centimetres, because 72 plus 60 plus 60 plus 48 comes to that
options.misconception: adds the four measurements instead of comparing the extremes

options.text: Twelve centimetres, because 60 cm on an arm of 72 cm is 12 cm shorter
options.misconception: compares the longest with an arm of average length

options.text: Twenty-four centimetres, because 72 cm on the longest arm less 48 cm on the shortest

questions.explanation: The longest arm is 72 cm and the shortest 48 cm, so the difference is 24 cm. Adding the four, comparing with an average arm, or setting two equal readings against each other answer other questions.
questions.hint: Compare the extreme readings on the graph.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The gold ground of the San Vitale apse, Ravenna
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a relationship between gold density and figure height expresses
questions.stem: Plotted against figure height, a graph of the San Vitale apse tracks the gold density of the conch and the height of the figures below it. Explain what the relationship between those two lines expresses about the design.

answer.exemplar: A gold field that grows denser as the figures beneath it grow taller ties the light of the gold directly to the scale of the sacred personages, so the heavens above answer in weight and brilliance to the figures below. The graph records two measurements and the relation between them, and the meaning comes from the convention that made the gold stand for uncreated light, not from the measurement itself.

questions.explanation: Gold that grows denser as the figures grow taller ties the light above to the scale of the figures below. The graph records two measurements; the convention carries the meaning.
questions.hint: Ask what the light above is answering to below.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The youthful shepherd in the Galla Placidia mosaics, Ravenna
questions.learningObjective: Describe a repeated figure type from a constant measured area

stimulus.body: A conservator's plot of the Galla Placidia mosaics shows the shepherd's figure appearing in each of four scenes, and the area each figure occupies is close to the same in every case. The sheep around it vary in number from three to nine. The report is to describe the shepherd's treatment across the four scenes.

questions.stem: Across four scenes of the Galla Placidia mosaics, a conservator's plot shows the shepherd's figure at a near constant area. Which treatment does the plot describe?

options.text: A portrait, because a specific figure would naturally be painted at a constant size
options.misconception: reads a constant size as evidence of a portrait likeness

options.text: A fixed and repeated type, held at a steady size while the flock around it is allowed to vary
A figure that grows with the flock, so that the larger flocks receive the larger shepherd
options.misconception: assumes the shepherd's size follows the number of sheep

options.text: An afterthought, added last to fill the gaps left by the animal groups
options.misconception: explains a constant size by a late addition

questions.explanation: A near constant area across four scenes with a varying flock describes a repeated type, held steady while the animals around it change. A constant size proves no portrait and no order of work.
questions.hint: Ask what stays fixed while the animals around the figure vary.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Encaustic handling in the Sinai icon of the Virgin and Child
questions.learningObjective: Set out the conditions for calling a handling painterly rather than linear
questions.stem: In the Sinai icon, a graph plots the thickness of the encaustic paint in the Virgin's face, in the drapery, and in the gold ground of the halo. Which two steps does a reader need before the handling is called painterly rather than linear?

options.text: Show the icon is the largest in the group, then treat the heavier paint as evidence of a richer pigment
options.misconception: explains paint thickness by the size of the panel

options.text: Show the halo is thinner, then treat the difference as a sign of a later campaign
options.misconception: reads a difference in thickness as a sign of a later campaign

options.text: Show the paint is built in separate strokes, then show the strokes model flesh and follow the form
Show the paint is warm in tone, then assume warmth alone makes a handling painterly
options.misconception: treats a warm palette as proof of a painterly hand

questions.explanation: A handling is painterly when the paint is built in visible strokes and those strokes follow the form. Colour, panel size and thickness describe the surface but not the method.
questions.hint: Ask what the individual strokes are doing to the form.
